title: Alert Thresholds: Extreme Value Theory
text:
Every window gets a reconstruction loss \(\ell(\mathbf{x})\) from the Detector. An alert fires when \(\ell(\mathbf{x}) > \tau_q\). Here \(\tau_q\) is the \(q\)-quantile threshold of the loss for normal windows: a normal window exceeds it with probability \(1 - q\). “The 99.9% threshold” therefore means an exceedance probability of 0.1% per normal window. It is not a confidence level. It is also not adaptive: \(\tau_q\) is estimated once and then fixed. Refitting it on a rolling window or by time of day is listed as further work.
Peaks over threshold (POT). Above a high level \(u\), the excesses \(\ell - u\) are modelled with a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) with scale \(\sigma\) and shape \(\xi\). With \(N\) windows, \(N_u\) of which exceed \(u\),
\[
\tau_q =
\begin{cases}
u + \dfrac{\sigma}{\xi}\left[\left(\dfrac{N}{N_u}(1-q)\right)^{-\xi} - 1\right], & \xi \neq 0,\\[2ex]
u + \sigma \ln\!\left(\dfrac{N_u}{N(1-q)}\right), & \xi = 0 .
\end{cases}
\]
The second line is the exponential limit. The code (gpd_tau() in R/evt.R) switches to it when \(|\xi| < 10^{-6}\), and a unit test checks that it returns a finite value at \(\xi = 0\).
Held-out fitting. The GPD is fitted to losses from the 4 validation hosts (16,128 windows), which the autoencoder never trained on. Training losses are biased low, because the model has seen those windows. Their fit is kept only as a comparison row. We set \(u\) at the 95% quantile.

Fitted parameters
Without the fitted parameters a reader can’t judge the shape of the tail or check the threshold arithmetic. The original report did not show them.

  fit = label, u = p$u, Nu = p$Nu, N = p$N,
  sigma = pm(p$sigma, p$se[["scale"]]), xi = pm(p$xi, p$se[["shape"]]),
  tau_990 = pot_taus(p, 0.99), tau_999 = pot_taus(p, 0.999),
  emp_990 = quantile(losses, 0.99), emp_999 = quantile(losses, 0.999)
)
bind_rows(

title: Alert Thresholds: Extreme Value Theory
text:
Threshold diagnostics
The choice of \(u\) and the GPD fit are assumptions. These plots test whether the assumptions are reasonable.


Display code
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
evd::mrlplot(main$loss_val, tlim = quantile(main$loss_val, c(0.80, 0.995)),
             main = "Mean residual life", xlab = "Threshold u")
abline(v = pot$u, lty = 2, col = "#e34948")
evd::tcplot(main$loss_val, tlim = quantile(main$loss_val, c(0.85, 0.99)), nt = 15,
            which = 1:2, std.err = TRUE)








Figure 1





How to read the plots. Left: the average amount by which losses exceed each candidate cut-off. Above a suitable cut-off this line should be roughly straight. Middle and right: the tail model’s adjusted scale and its shape \(\xi\), refitted at fifteen cut-offs between the 85% and 99% quantiles, with 95% intervals as vertical bars. A suitable cut-off is one above which these estimates stay flat. The dashed red line marks the cut-off actually chosen.
What the plots tell you. There is no stable region. The shape estimate keeps rising with the cut-off, from 0.19 at the 90% quantile to 0.68 at the 99% quantile, and the mean-excess line curves upward instead of straightening. One smooth tail model does not describe these losses well, because they mix ordinary errors with discrete count spikes. The chosen cut-off is a compromise, and the 99.9% threshold moves between 3.29 and 3.71 depending on it.


Display code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(pot$fit, which = c(2, 4))








Figure 2





How to read the plots. Left: each point compares an observed tail loss with the value the fitted model predicts for it, and points on the diagonal mean a good fit. Right: the loss level the model implies for increasingly rare events, moving right on a logarithmic scale, with observed losses as crosses and dotted 95% bands. Bands that widen quickly mean the model is uncertain about how large the rarest losses can get.
What the plots tell you. The points follow the line through the body of the tail, then jump in a visible step: the cluster of count-spike windows that the smooth model cannot represent. Above that step the observed losses fall below the fitted curve, so the model may overstate the most extreme thresholds. The bands fan out quickly to the right, so thresholds for very rare events are far less certain than the 99.9% threshold used for alerts.

title: Alert Thresholds: Extreme Value Theory
text:
Clustering of alerts
Exceedances are not independent: one busy period produces several high-loss windows in a row. The extremal index \(\theta\) measures this. \(1/\theta\) is the average number of exceedances per cluster. We estimate it with the runs method: exceedances within 3 windows of each other belong to one cluster.


Display code

tibble(q = q[1:3]) |>
  mutate(
    q_lab = paste0(formatC(100 * q, format = "f", digits = 2), "%"),
    windows = (1 - q) * vol,
    incidents = theta * windows
  ) |>
  select(q_lab, windows, incidents) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "From Window Exceedances to Distinct Alert Clusters",
             subtitle = sprintf("Extremal index θ = %.2f; volume %s windows per day", theta, f_int(vol))) |>
  cols_label(q_lab = "Quantile q", windows = "Normal windows alerting / day", incidents = "Distinct clusters / day") |>

title: Service Dependency Graph
text:
The detector on the Detector page scores each host’s activity in 5-minute windows. It says nothing about what happens if the security team responds by isolating that host. Isolating a host that many other services depend on can cause an outage that does more damage than the attack. This page builds the structural layer that answers that question. It ranks services by how much of the enterprise depends on them. The ranking feeds a containment rule on the Evaluation page: alerts on the most critical services go to a human before any automated isolation.
The graph is simulated: 23 services and 42 dependencies, with call volumes drawn from a log-normal distribution. A real deployment would build it from service-mesh or API-gateway call logs.

The detector on the Detector page scores each host’s activity in 5-minute windows. It says nothing about what happens if the security team responds by isolating that host. Isolating a host that many other services depend on can cause an outage that does more damage than the attack. This page builds the structural layer that answers that question. It ranks services by how much of the enterprise depends on them. The ranking feeds a containment rule on the Evaluation page: alerts on the most critical services go to a human before any automated isolation.
The graph is simulated: 23 services and 42 dependencies, with call volumes drawn from a log-normal distribution. A real deployment would build it from service-mesh or API-gateway call logs.

title: Service Dependency Graph
text:
Definitions
Edge direction. An edge \(i \to j\) means service \(i\) calls (depends on) service \(j\). The edge weight \(w_{ij}\) is the call volume over a fixed period.
Markov transition matrix. Follow one request as it moves from service to service. The probability that the next call goes to \(j\), given that the request is at \(i\), is
\[P_{ij} = \Pr(X_{t+1} = j \mid X_t = i) = \frac{w_{ij}}{\sum_k w_{ik}},\]
so every row of \(P\) sums to 1 (row-stochastic). Services that call nothing (for example the key-management service) are dangling. Their rows are set to \(1/n\), the standard convention: a request that reaches a dead end restarts anywhere.
The Markov (memoryless) assumption. The next hop depends only on the current service, not on how the request got there. Real request paths are often session-dependent (authentication, then API, then database), so this is an approximation. With real call traces it can be tested by comparing the fit of first- and second-order transition models. This simulation has no traces, so the assumption is stated, not tested.
PageRank. PageRank is the stationary distribution \(\pi\) of the walk with random restarts:
\[\pi = \alpha\, \pi P + \frac{1-\alpha}{n}\mathbf{1}^\top .\]
\(\pi_j\) is the long-run share of request hops that land on service \(j\). We call this dependency concentration. It is not the probability that a failure spreads to \(j\), and it does not detect single points of failure by itself. The damping factor \(\alpha\) is the chance the walk follows a call rather than restarting. The value \(\alpha = 0.85\) is a web-search convention, not a risk parameter, so we test how sensitive the ranking is to it.
Single points of failure are a connectivity question, so we measure them directly:

Articulation points: services whose removal disconnects the graph (treating edges as undirected).
Betweenness: how many shortest dependency paths pass through a service.
Removal impact: remove the service and count the share of the other services that can no longer reach at least one dependency they could reach before.

How to read the table. Each row is a check that the calculation behaved as intended. The first confirms every row of the transition matrix sums to one, so each service’s outgoing calls form a proper probability split. The second and third show how many repeated passes the ranking needed before it stopped changing, and how small the last change was. The final row compares our hand-written ranking with igraph, a widely used network-analysis library.
What the table tells you. The calculation is sound. The row sums are exact to rounding error, the ranking settled after 39 passes, and the result agrees with igraph to within 1e-13, which is effectively identical. That matters because the criticality tiers that govern containment decisions rest on these numbers. An error here would silently route the wrong alerts to automation instead of to a person, and nothing downstream would reveal it.
Damping sensitivity. Re-ranking the services at \(\alpha \in \{0.75, 0.85, 0.95\}\) gives a Kendall rank correlation with the \(\alpha = 0.85\) ranking of at least 1.000. On this graph the ranking does not depend on the damping choice, although the PageRank values themselves do.

title: Service Dependency Graph
text:
Dependency map
The map shows which services the rest of the enterprise funnels into. A security response that isolates one of these services can take down everything upstream of it.


Display code
set.seed(cfg$graph$seed)
ggraph(g, layout = "sugiyama") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = calls), alpha = 0.35, colour = "#52514e",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.5, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    end_cap = circle(4, "mm")
  ) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = pagerank, colour = tier)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), size = 3.4, repel = TRUE, colour = "#0b0b0b",
                 bg.colour = "white", bg.r = 0.15, point.padding = unit(3, "mm")) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2), name = "Call volume") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 14, name = "PageRank") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = tier_colors, name = "Criticality tier") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))) +
  labs(
    title = "Simulated Service Dependency Graph",
    subtitle = "Arrows point from caller to dependency; node size = PageRank (dependency concentration)"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 10))








Figure 1





How to read the plot. Each dot is a service, and each arrow points from a service to something it depends on: the caller sits at the tail, the dependency at the head. Entry points such as the web portal and mobile app sit at the top, and shared platform services sit at the bottom. Larger dots carry more request traffic in the long run (PageRank), thicker arrows carry more calls, and colour shows the criticality tier assigned further down the page.
What the plot tells you. Traffic converges on a handful of shared platform services: Key Management, File Store, DNS Resolver have the highest PageRank. Nobody uses these services directly, so they are easy to overlook, yet nearly everything else depends on them. Isolating one in response to an alert could take down much of the estate. The two articulation points, API Gateway and Customer Service, matter for a different reason: removing either splits the map into disconnected pieces.

title: Service Dependency Graph
section: Criticality tiers and the containment rule
text:
Criticality tiers and the containment rule
The tiers are a policy choice built from the measures above:

Tier 1: an articulation point, or removal cuts off at least 50% of the other services. This gives 6 services: Key Management, File Store, DNS Resolver, API Gateway, Notification Svc, Customer Service.
Tier 2: PageRank at or above the median, and not Tier 1 (7 services).
Tier 3: everything else (10 services).

Containment rule. An alert on a Tier 1 asset requires human approval before any isolation or credential revocation, because isolating it is itself an outage. Tier 2 and Tier 3 assets may get automated low-blast-radius actions (step-up authentication, ending a single session) while an analyst reviews. Automated host isolation stays off for every tier until the detector has been validated on production data. The Evaluation page applies this rule to the simulated alerts.

title: Service Dependency Graph
text:
Limitations of this layer
The graph, call volumes and tiers are illustrative. Removal impact treats every dependency as hard: a service is counted as impacted if it loses any dependency, with no allowance for caches, retries or failover replicas. The tier cut-offs are judgment calls and should be set with the service owners. A production version would build \(P\) from observed call logs, test the first-order Markov assumption against session traces, and check the tiers against past incidents.

title: Cyber Anomaly Detection & Service Dependency Risk
text:
Signature rules and fixed thresholds miss attacks that stay inside normal ranges. This project tests a two-layer alternative, built in R, on simulated enterprise telemetry.
The structural layer models 23 services as a Markov transition matrix of call flows. It ranks them by PageRank, articulation points and a node-removal simulation, and turns the ranking into criticality tiers that decide which alerts may trigger automated containment.
The detection layer is a shallow autoencoder, written in base R with analytic gradients and Adam. It is trained on 19 correlated, seasonal telemetry features. Alerts fire when reconstruction loss exceeds a threshold fitted to the loss tail with a Generalized Pareto Distribution on held-out hosts.
Results. Across 30 independent seeds (mean [95% range]):

The autoencoder separates attacks from normal windows with ROC AUC 0.794 [0.734–0.824]. Mahalanobis distance does better (0.817 [0.765–0.843]), so the network adds nothing over simpler statistics on this data.
At the 99.9% threshold it catches 77.0% [63.8%–82.0%] of high-intensity attacks, 24.6% [19.1%–34.3%] of medium and 0.8% [0.2%–2.1%] of low.
It misses data exfiltration at every intensity.
False alarms at 99.9% were 14.1 [1.5–52.2] per 8,064 normal windows, against about 8 expected. The threshold does not transfer cleanly to new hosts.
The loss tail is heavy (shape ξ = 0.24 [0.10–0.38]), driven by rare benign count spikes.

The two-layer design is sound. The detector, as built, is not ready for automated response.
These results come from simulated data and injected attacks, not production telemetry. They show how the method behaves, not how it would perform in a real enterprise.

title: Cyber Anomaly Detection & Service Dependency Risk
text:
Introduction
Enterprise systems produce large volumes of authentication, network and host telemetry. Most monitoring still relies on fixed signatures and static thresholds, which miss attacks that stay inside normal ranges. Credential stuffing spread across many sources and slow data exfiltration are examples. An unsupervised detector learns what normal looks like and flags departures from it, so it can in principle catch attacks nobody has written a rule for.
Detection alone is not enough. The usual response to an alert is containment: isolate a host, revoke a token. If the affected service sits under much of the estate, the containment can cause a larger outage than the attack. This project therefore pairs the detector with a structural model of service dependencies. Together they answer two questions: is this window abnormal? and how dangerous is it to act on that automatically?






WarningRead this first



Every number on this site comes from a simulation with assumed parameters (params.yaml). The results show how the methods behave under controlled conditions. They do not estimate how the system would perform on any real network.

title: Cyber Anomaly Detection & Service Dependency Risk
text:
Techniques
Markov transition matrix. Services are nodes, and an edge \(i \to j\) means service \(i\) calls service \(j\). Normalizing call volumes by row gives \(P_{ij} = \Pr(\text{next call goes to } j \mid \text{at } i)\), a row-stochastic matrix. It assumes the next hop depends only on the current service (first-order Markov). Details →
PageRank. PageRank is the long-run share of request hops landing on each service, with random restarts weighted by a damping factor. It measures dependency concentration. It is not a single-point-of-failure detector, so it is cross-checked against articulation points and a node-removal simulation.
Shallow autoencoder. A 19-4-19 network with a \(\tanh\) bottleneck and a linear decoder, trained only on normal windows. Each window is scored by its mean squared reconstruction error \(\ell(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac{1}{d}\lVert \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}} \rVert^2\). With one hidden layer it is close to principal component analysis, and the results confirm this. Details →
Extreme Value Theory (peaks over threshold). Losses above a high level are modelled with a Generalized Pareto Distribution. This gives quantile thresholds \(\tau_q\) for exceedance probabilities too small to estimate directly from the data. The thresholds come with bootstrap intervals, diagnostics and a calibration test. Details →

title: Cyber Anomaly Detection & Service Dependency Risk
text:
Recommendations
We recommend three governance practices:

Human-in-the-loop containment, routed by criticality. Alerts on Tier 1 services (Key Management, File Store, DNS Resolver, API Gateway, Notification Svc, Customer Service) require human approval before isolation or credential revocation, because isolating them is itself an outage. Automate only low-blast-radius actions, such as step-up authentication or ending a single session, and only after the detector has been validated on production telemetry. At realistic attack rates most alerts at the 99.9% threshold would be false alarms (see the base-rate table), so automated isolation today would mostly hit healthy hosts.
Explain every alert, and test the explanations. Report the top three contributing features with each alert. Measure how often they point at the true cause, and compare them against plain z-scores, which did as well here. This aligns with the explainability and model-risk expectations in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (voluntary) and OSFI Guideline E-23 (effective May 1, 2027 for federally regulated Canadian financial institutions). Neither one prescribes a specific detector.
Monitor drift by effect size, not significance. Replace weekly per-feature KS tests with Wasserstein distance per feature (in standard-deviation units, with an effect-size trigger). Track the live alert rate against its expected \(1-q\), and refit and re-validate the threshold on a schedule. In the drift test, KS flagged harmless shifts every time, and PSI at standard cut-offs missed a material one.

title: Cyber Anomaly Detection & Service Dependency Risk
text:
Limitations
What would change the conclusions:

Simulated data. The latent factors, marginals, correlations, seasonality and host roles are all assumptions. Real telemetry has missing data, logging changes, holidays and populations of very different hosts. Client data would replace the generator in R/sim.R: at least four weeks of host-by-window telemetry with an asset inventory.
Simulated attacks. Each attack changes a few features in single windows or short runs. Real campaigns move across hosts and over days. Labelled red-team or incident data would replace params.yaml: attacks.
Heavy, discrete tail. Rare count features dominate extreme normal losses, so a single GPD fits poorly and the threshold depends on the chosen level \(u\). Per-host or per-role thresholds, or separate models for count features, may change the picture.
Fixed threshold. \(\tau_q\) is fitted once. Thresholds that adapt over time, by rolling refit or by time of day, are not implemented.
Dependency graph. The graph, call volumes and tier cut-offs are illustrative. The first-order Markov assumption is stated, not tested. Service-mesh call logs and session traces would replace them.
Prevalence. The test set is about 28% attacks. Real environments are orders of magnitude lower, which is why the base-rate table matters more than the ROC curve.

title: Detector: Simulation & Shallow Autoencoder
text:
Telemetry generator
The original version of this study drew all 16 features independently. With independent, unit-variance inputs, a 4-unit bottleneck can at best keep 4 of 16 dimensions, so the lowest achievable reconstruction error was \(12/16 = 0.75\). That was exactly where the old training curve flattened. The plateau did not show the model learning business patterns. It showed the model hitting the floor for data with no structure to learn.
The generator now has structure. Each feature is driven by shared latent factors through a Gaussian copula:

Business activity follows a daily cycle peaking at 13:00, is lower at weekends (30% of the weekday peak), and has AR(1) persistence (\(\phi = 0.5\)).
Host workload, plus shared network-volume, authentication-volume and process-activity factors, each AR(1) with \(\phi = 0.5\).
Host role, a constant per host, so hosts differ from one another, as real fleets do.

For each window the latent factors plus independent noise give correlated standard-normal scores. pnorm() turns these into uniforms, and the quantile function of each target distribution (qpois, qlnorm, qbeta, …) maps them onto realistic marginals. Three features were added to support a real lateral-movement scenario: new destination hosts, SMB/RDP/WinRM connections and new service creations. That makes \(d = 19\).

title: Detector: Simulation & Shallow Autoencoder
text:
Preprocessing
A recipes pipeline applies a Yeo-Johnson transform and then standardizes each feature to zero mean and unit variance. Both steps are estimated on the training hosts only and applied unchanged to validation and test windows, so no information leaks from evaluation data.

title: Detector: Simulation & Shallow Autoencoder
text:
Shallow autoencoder
Architecture. Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}\) be a batch of \(N\) windows across \(d = 19\) features. The encoder maps to a \(k = 4\)-unit bottleneck with a \(\tanh\) activation, and a linear decoder maps back:
\[Z = \tanh\left(X W_e + \mathbf{1}_N \mathbf{b}_e^\top\right), \qquad \hat{X} = Z W_d + \mathbf{1}_N \mathbf{b}_d^\top,\]
with \(W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\), \(\mathbf{b}_e \in \mathbb{R}^k\), \(W_d \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}\), \(\mathbf{b}_d \in \mathbb{R}^d\). One hidden layer with a linear decoder is a shallow autoencoder, close to principal component analysis. The sensitivity table below confirms this.
Loss. Training minimizes the batch mean squared error, and each window is scored by its own mean squared error over features:
\[\mathcal{L}(X, \hat{X}) = \frac{1}{N d}\,\lVert X - \hat{X} \rVert_F^2, \qquad \ell(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{d}\,\lVert \mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}} \rVert^2 .\]
Gradients. By matrix calculus,
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{X}} = \frac{2}{N d}(\hat{X} - X), \quad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_d} = Z^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{X}}, \quad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}_d} = \mathbf{1}_N^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{X}},\]
\[\Delta_Z = \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{X}} W_d^\top\right) \odot (1 - Z^2), \quad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_e} = X^\top \Delta_Z, \quad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{b}_e} = \mathbf{1}_N^\top \Delta_Z .\]
Parameters are updated with Adam (bias-corrected first and second moments, learning rate 0.005, batch size 256) from Xavier-initialized weights. Training stops early when validation loss has not improved for 5 epochs, and the best weights are kept. The implementation (R/ae.R) handles any stack of \(\tanh\) layers, which the sensitivity check uses.

Figure 1





How to read the plot. Each panel is one attack intensity tier. Each box shows the spread of reconstruction loss for one attack type: the middle line is the median, the box spans the middle half of windows, and the dots are unusual values. Grey is normal traffic, repeated in every panel. The horizontal axis is logarithmic. Anything to the right of the dashed line triggers an alert at the 99.9% threshold, and the dotted line is the 99% threshold.
What the plot tells you. Normal windows have a median loss of 0.506 and a 99th percentile of 1.728. Low-intensity attacks look exactly like normal traffic. At high intensity, credential stuffing, privilege escalation, ransomware staging and lateral movement clear the alert line. Exfiltration does not, even at the high tier, because large changes to a few features are diluted in a 19-feature average. Low-and-slow exfiltration sits wholly inside the normal range.

text:
Detection frontiers
The curves show detection against false alarms at every possible threshold, for the autoencoder and for simpler alternatives.


Display code
truth <- factor(if_else(is_att, "Anomaly", "Normal"), levels = c("Anomaly", "Normal"))
curves <- imap(main$scores_test, \(s, m) {

    roc = yardstick::roc_curve(df, truth, score, event_level = "first") |> mutate(method = m),
    pr = yardstick::pr_curve(df, truth, score, event_level = "first") |> mutate(method = m)
  )
})

  ggplot(aes(1 - specificity, sensitivity, colour = method)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c3c2b7") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "ROC Frontier", x = "False-positive rate", y = "True-positive rate")
p_pr <- map(curves, "pr") |> bind_rows() |>
  ggplot(aes(recall, precision, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(is_att), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#c3c2b7") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = method_colors, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Precision-Recall Frontier", x = "Recall", y = "Precision")
(p_roc + p_pr) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2





How to read the plots. Left: the share of attacks caught against the share of normal windows wrongly flagged, as the threshold slides from strict to loose. Curves nearer the top-left are better, and the dashed diagonal is random guessing. Right: the share of alerts that are real (precision) against the share of attacks caught (recall). The dashed line marks the attack share in this test set, 27.9%, far above any real environment.
What the plots tell you. All six methods trace almost the same curves. The autoencoder’s ROC AUC is 0.792, and the best method on this run is Mahalanobis distance at 0.819. Every ROC curve rises steeply and then flattens, because low-intensity attacks look like normal traffic to every method. Precision looks respectable only because attacks make up 27.9% of this test set. The base-rate table below shows realistic prevalence.

Most attack types light up a feature the attack actually changed: source IPs for credential stuffing, privilege escalations for privilege escalation, DNS queries and file writes for ransomware staging, and new service creations for lateral movement. The few exfiltration windows that were detected are different. Their darkest cell is an unrelated spike, not bytes or session length, so they were flagged for the wrong reason. The last column repeats it using each feature’s plain distance from average, with no model involved. “Detected windows” shows how many alerts each percentage rests on.
What the table tells you. Wherever there are enough detections to judge, both methods place a changed feature in the top three every time. Attribution works, but it does not need the autoencoder: plain distance from average does just as well. The test is also lenient. The exfiltration windows count as hits because a changed feature ranks second or third, although the alert was driven by something else. A stricter top-one test would be more informative.

Drift monitoring
The original recommendation was a weekly Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test on every feature at \(p < 0.01\). This table tests that rule and two alternatives on a simulated week from 100 new hosts (201,600 windows).

How to read the table. Each row is one version of a simulated new week: unchanged, with two features nudged by a trivial 0.05 standard deviations, or by a material 0.3. The KS columns count features that a significance test flags as changed. PSI is a common stability index, read as “watch” above 0.1 and “act” above 0.2. What the table tells you. The significance test fails both ways. It flags the trivial shift as firmly as the material one, and it flags 3 untouched features in every scenario because new hosts differ slightly. PSI misses the material shift (maximum 0.089). Wasserstein distance reads the shift size directly and separates trivial from material. The alert rate barely moved, so it cannot be the only monitor either.
